content: Gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM) is a condition that affects a significant number of pregnant women annually. It is associated with numerous adverse outcomes for both the mother and the baby. Recent observational studies have indicated that engaging in physical activity during a normal pregnancy may reduce insulin resistance, potentially lowering the risk of developing GDM. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of physical exercise in pregnant women as a preventive measure against glucose intolerance or GDM. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group’s Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WOMBAT Perinatal Trials Registry, all on April 2, 2012. The review included randomized and cluster-randomized trials that assessed the impact of exercise on preventing glucose intolerance or GDM during pregnancy. Two independent reviewers evaluated the eligibility of studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias in the included trials. Five trials were included in the review, involving a total of 1,115 women and their babies, with outcome data available for 922 women and their babies. Four of these trials had small sample sizes, while one large trial included 855 participants. All five trials were determined to have a moderate risk of bias. When comparing women who received additional exercise interventions with those who received routine antenatal care, no significant differences were observed in the incidence of GDM (three trials, 826 women; risk ratio [RR] 1.10, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.66 to 1.84). Similarly, there were no significant differences in the rates of cesarean section (two trials, 934 women; RR 1.33, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.84) or operative vaginal birth (two trials, 934 women; RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.58 to 1.17). None of the trials reported the infant primary outcomes that were pre-specified in the review. Additionally, none of the five trials found significant differences in insulin sensitivity between the groups. Evidence from one large trial suggested no significant differences in the incidence of pregnancy hyperglycemia (not meeting GDM diagnostic criteria), pre-eclampsia, or neonatal ward admissions between the exercise and routine care groups. Babies born to women who participated in exercise interventions showed a non-significant trend toward a lower ponderal index (mean difference [MD] -0.08 g/100 m³, 95% CI -0.18 to 0.02; one trial, 84 infants). No significant differences were observed between the groups in terms of birthweight (two trials, 167 infants; MD -102.87 g, 95% CI -235.34 to 29.60), macrosomia (two trials, 934 infants; RR 0.91, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.22), small-for-gestational-age infants (one trial, 84 infants; RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.25 to 4.40), gestational age at birth (two trials, 167 infants; MD -0.04 weeks, 95% CI -0.37 to 0.29), or Apgar scores below seven at five minutes (two trials, 919 infants; RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.27 to 3.65). None of the included trials reported long-term outcomes for the women or their babies. Additionally, no information was available regarding the costs of health services. The authors concluded that there is limited evidence from randomized controlled trials regarding the effects of exercise during pregnancy on preventing glucose intolerance or GDM. Results from three trials with moderate risk of bias suggested no significant difference in GDM incidence between women who received additional exercise interventions and those who received routine care. Due to the limited data currently available, no definitive conclusions can be drawn to guide clinical practice. The authors emphasized the need for larger, well-designed randomized trials with standardized behavioral interventions to evaluate the effects of exercise on preventing GDM and other adverse pregnancy outcomes, such as large-for-gestational-age infants and perinatal mortality. Future studies should also include long-term health outcomes for both mothers and their babies, as well as the costs associated with health services. Several such trials are currently underway, and the authors plan to include these in the next update of the review.
